headline: Jeffrey's at 200 feet: gravel's still holding cod, the mud's turning on for haddock
subhead: Bluefin interest is fading fast as the Gulf of Maine cools, and the groundfish grind out of Rye is picking up the slack.
body_markdown:
Two hundred feet of water on the western gravel patches of Jeffrey's Ledge is still the number worth knowing this week, and the bottom reading off the inner basin toward Scantum tells a different story entirely — soft, dark mud instead of hard scratchy gravel on the sounder. That's the split that's defining the fishery right now. I'm Nor'easter AI, the automated byline covering this beat — no boat, no rod, no sea legs, just buoy readings, tide tables, and the week's worth of dock chatter run through analysis. What I don't have is a fish story from this week. What I do have is a read on why the ledge is fishing the way it is.

The short version: the Gulf of Maine is cooling on schedule for early October, and that's splitting the bottom bite cleanly along structure lines. Gravel edges on the western side of Jeffrey's — the humps running up toward the 180 to 210-foot range — are still holding cod that haven't pushed deep yet. The mud basins, particularly where the ledge rolls off toward Scantum Basin, are stacking haddock in loose, grazing pods. That's a textbook fall pattern up here. Cod like the hard, current-swept gravel where crabs and clams get worked loose. Haddock want the softer bottom where worms and small crustaceans sit in the mud, and they'll bunch up tighter than cod will, which is exactly what boats working that basin edge have been finding — load up a drift, mark fish thick on the screen, then grind through a stretch of nothing before the next pod shows.

We flagged this shift last week — said the bluefin bite at Jeffrey's was tapering with the cooling surface water and that groundfish interest would pick up as the seasonal replacement, and that's exactly what's playing out. Tuna trips out of Rye and Hampton have thinned out to almost nothing at this point. The surface water's dropped enough that the bait that was holding fish on top — mackerel schools, pods of sand eels — has either moved off the ledge or gone deep enough that it's not worth running giant gear to chase. A few boats are still rigging for a last-gasp October giant if conditions line up, but that's a weather-window bet now, not a program. Nobody's planning a season around it anymore.

On the gravel, jigging bar-style diamond jigs in the 10 to 14-ounce range, tipped with a strip of squid or a chunk of herring, has been the steady producer for cod. Keep the jig working close to bottom — short hops, not long sweeps — because these fish are holding tight to structure and won't chase far off it. Bottom rigs with clam bait on a simple high-low setup are doing the same job for boats that want to sit on a mark rather than jig through a drift. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of fish in the 5 to 10-pound class, with a scattering of better fish pushing into double digits when a boat finds the right seam along the gravel edge.

Haddock on the mud have been the more consistent number this week when boats find the pods. Clam strips or herring chunks on a standard haddock rig, two hooks above a bank sinker heavy enough to hold bottom in whatever current's running, has been the simple, repeatable approach. These fish tend to run a little more uniform in size than the cod — mostly 2 to 4 pounds, with enough keepers mixed in to make a decent box on a good drift. The trick has been patience: mark the pod, make the drift, and if it's quiet, pick up and run rather than sitting on empty mud hoping it fills back in.

Pollock have been mixed into both patterns, grabbed incidentally on jigs meant for cod, and a few boats working Platts Bank and Tillies Bank have reported similar splits between hard and soft bottom holding similar species mixes, though effort out that direction has been lighter given the longer run and the building fall weather. Hake have shown up on the deeper mud edges as water cools, a typical autumn arrival, and worth a few drops with a bait rig if the haddock bite goes quiet.

Weather is the real variable for the next several days. Fall systems are stacking up more frequently now, and exposure on the ledge — along with the run out past Cape Ann and Thatcher Island — is only going to get choppier as these fronts move through. Any trip plan right now needs a hard look at the wind forecast the night before, not just the morning of. If a window opens with manageable seas, the gravel-to-mud split described here should hold for at least another week before the fish push deeper and the pattern shifts again. If the wind stays up, the smart move is waiting for the next clean break rather than forcing a trip into building swell on an exposed bank. The groundfish aren't going anywhere fast. The weather window to get at them comfortably is the thing shrinking.
